TODDLER ROOM LESSON · TODDLER ROOM · AGES 1–3 YEARS

Crayons — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches "crayons" through a shared scribble — one crayon each, marks on paper, and the golden question: "tell me about your drawing."

What is this?

Crayons are the wax sticks that make colored marks on paper — the first drawing tools, and at this age the marks are scribbles with narratives attached.

What does it mean?

Scribbling is pre-writing and the narration is pre-literacy: a child who explains a scribble is learning that marks carry meaning, which is the whole secret of reading waiting downstream.

What does the child need to know?

You need paper taped down (the tape IS the trick — no sliding, no floor art), one crayon per hand and the question rule: "tell me about it," never "what is it?"

Why this matters

Being asked to narrate makes the child the author. Being asked to identify makes them the test-taker. Same scribble, opposite lessons — choose author.

What it teaches

Tripod grip seeds, mark control (pressure, direction), color words, narrative language and the sitting-focus that pencil work will later borrow.

Words to learn

crayonscolorsscribbledrawpapertell me

Say this to your child

“"Crayons! Let’s draw. Pick a crayon… I have green. Scribble, scribble! Look at the colors. Now — tell me about your drawing. Oh! It’s a car going to grandma’s? Tell me more!"”

Step by step

  1. Tape the paper, open the box: "crayons! Look at the colors — red, yellow, green, blue."
  2. Each choose one: "I pick green. You pick…?" — choice first, name second.
  3. Scribble side by side in silence for a minute. Companionable noise from the crayons only.
  4. Ask the golden question about THEIR page: "tell me about your drawing!" Listen. Follow the story wherever it goes — cars, monsters, grandma.
  5. Date and display: pin it up, or fridge-front it. An audience keeps authors writing.

Look closer at the picture

On this card the word "crayons" sits under five crayons standing in a yellow-and-green box — the toolkit, packed and ready.

Ask your child

"Which color is that?" "Tell me about your drawing!" "Can you make a big circle? A fast line?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might name colors while scribbling, narrate the story ("it’s a dog… running!"), or hand you a crayon and demand you draw — all of it is authorship.

Out in the real world

Color and mark live everywhere: the menu at the restaurant, chalk on the pavement, the shopping list. "I need my crayons for THAT!" is the sound of the word working.

Try it together

Story Gallery: three drawings, pinned in a row. A tour guide (the artist) walks you past each one and tells its story. Tickets are optional; pride is not.

Understanding check

Ask: "What are these?" (crayons) "Which color?" "Tell me about your picture!" — name, choose, narrate: the writer’s first lesson is done.

This lesson pairs with the Crayons flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Toddler Room.
